analysis.one_liner: Bars mining waste from being dumped into streams and valleys as "fill" under clean water law.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop mining waste from being dumped into streams drew 153 House cosponsors but never got a committee vote and died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how the Clean Water Act defines "fill material." Under it, any pollutant dumped into a river, lake, or stream primarily to get rid of waste would no longer count as legal "fill." That matters most for mountaintop-removal coal mining, in which companies blast off whole mountaintops and push the leftover rock and dirt into nearby valleys and streams; under current rules those waste dumps are permitted as "fill," and the bill would close that route.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near mountaintop-removal mining sites in Appalachia, whose drinking water and streams are contaminated by mining waste dumps, gain the most. Broader benefits go to anyone who uses or values clean rivers and streams, and to downstream communities that would no longer receive mining waste through the fill-permit loophole.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities living near mountaintop-removal coal mining

how_it_helps.text: It redefines "fill material" to mean anything that replaces waters of the United States with dry land or changes a water body's bottom elevation, but excludes any pollutant discharged primarily to dispose of waste [S2].

The bill's stated purpose is to clarify that fill material cannot be made of waste, closing the loophole under which mining waste dumped into streams is treated the same as ordinary construction fill [S3].

For the coal-mining practice of filling valleys and streams with excess rock from mountaintop removal, this would remove the existing permit route that allows those waste dumps, which is how the bill was understood to effectively end the practice (general knowledge of how Clean Water Act fill permits work).

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies that use mountaintop removal would bear the cost, since they could no longer dispose of excess rock and dirt by dumping it into valleys and streams as "fill." Some coal-mining jobs in Appalachia depend on that disposal method and would be at risk; opponents argued electricity costs could rise as a result.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is economic: mountaintop removal with valley fills is a disposal method the coal industry depends on, so ending it would eliminate some coal-mining jobs in Appalachian communities that already have few alternatives (general knowledge of how the disposal method relates to mining jobs).

The bill takes a blunt approach: it does not create a transition program or compensation for workers and towns that depend on mountaintop-removal mining, so the local economic cost would fall on those communities while the water-quality benefits flow broadly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is clean water for the communities that live directly below mining waste dumps, which is concrete and local. The cost is real but narrower: lost mining jobs and cheaper coal disposal in the affected region. An honest weighing favors the bill for those downstream communities, but the bill's weakness is that it offers nothing for the workers whose jobs depend on the practice it would end.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it to a committee, the committee sent it to a subcommittee, and neither ever took it up, so it died when the session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 3, 2007 by Rep. Frank Pallone and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it stayed [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no vote, no floor action through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S5].
By the end, the bill had 153 cosponsors, including 8 Republicans alongside 145 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mountaintop-removal coal companies came out ahead: the waste-dumping practice the bill would have ended continued, because the bill never advanced past its subcommittee referral. Communities near the mine sites gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 3, 2007 and recruited a large original cosponsor list [S1].

for.name: 153 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including 8 Republicans and 145 Democrats, but none could move the bill out of committee [S4].

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and never scheduled a markup or vote during the two-year Congress [S5].

against.name: Coal mining industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against restrictions on mountaintop-removal waste disposal, which the bill would have curtailed; no opponent action appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic (145 of 153 cosponsors) but included 8 Republicans, giving the bill some genuine cross-party backing; no member is recorded in opposition because no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill removes the permit route that lets these companies dispose of mining waste by dumping it into valleys and streams as "fill." That disposal method is central to mountaintop removal, so the bill targets the practice directly; the industry's interest in keeping it runs against the water quality of nearby communities.

Restricting a low-cost mining method could raise coal supply costs over time, though some of those costs might be passed to electricity customers. The effect is indirect and the bill does not regulate utilities.
